title: EARS Unwanted-Behaviour Requirements: Where Requirements for AI Agents Go Missing

Requirements Engineering Software Engineering Artificial Intelligence Software Development Product Management EARS Unwanted-Behaviour Requirements: Where Requirements for AI Agents Go Missing Nicolas Payette 7 min read · Oct 5, 2026 -- Listen Share Author’s note: this story was drafted with AI writing assistance, from research published on specira.ai. Press enter or click to view image in full size Picture a Tuesday afternoon, around 4:40. A coding agent picks up a ticket that reads, in full: “The client should retry failed requests.” It asks nothing. Twenty minutes later there is a pull request with a retry loop, green tests, and a reviewer who approves it because the code does exactly what the sentence says, which is almost nothing. How many retries, how long to wait between them, which failures count as retryable, and what exactly the caller sees when the very last attempt fails? The agent answered all four. Nobody saw it. My thesis: the requirements AI agents get wrong most often are the unwanted-behaviour ones, because humans rarely write them, and the EARS “If … then” pattern makes their absence visible without ever proving they are right. Why does an AI agent fill gaps a human teammate would ask about? A human developer reading “retry failed requests” walks over to someone’s desk. An agent does not. It treats the sentence as complete, picks the most ordinary interpretation it can find, and keeps going, because finishing is the job and stopping to question a requirement looks, from inside the loop, like failing. The Specira article How Do You Write a Requirement an AI Agent Cannot Misread? makes this case in more depth. Ambiguity used to cost a conversation; with an agent, it costs a silent decision. Those silent decisions tend to cluster on the failure path. Happy paths get described in user stories, demos and acceptance criteria, while the “what if it breaks” branch is where everyone assumes somebody else wrote it down. Usually nobody did. Press enter or click to view image in full size What is the EARS “If … then” pattern, and why is it the one that matters? EARS stands for the Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax. Alistair Mavin, Philip Wilkinson, Adrian Harwood and Mark Novak, working at Rolls-Royce, presented it at the 2009 Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) International Requirements Engineering Conference ( RE ‘09 ), using aero engine control system requirements from an airworthiness regulation document as their case study. Their abstract makes a modest claim. A small set of structural rules addresses eight common requirement problems, ambiguity, complexity and vagueness among them, so that each requirement can be expressed in one of five simple templates. Mavin’s own summary lists them: Ubiquitous (no keyword): always active. State-driven (While): active during a state. Event-driven (When): fires on a trigger. Optional feature (Where): applies when a feature is present. Unwanted behaviour (If … then): the response when something goes wrong. Complex requirements combine keywords, and the clause order is fixed: While precondition, When trigger, the system shall response. Mavin’s unwanted-behaviour example is almost boring: “If an invalid credit card number is entered, then the website shall display ‘please re-enter credit card details’.” Boring is the point. The keyword “If” forces a writer to name the bad thing, and “then” forces them to commit to a response, two decisions that many specifications skip entirely. This is not academic trivia, either. Kiro, the agentic development environment from Amazon Web Services (AWS), documents that its requirements.md uses EARS in the form WHEN [condition/event] THE SYSTEM SHALL [expected behavior]. Agents already read it. The “If” keyword is a question you cannot answer by accident. Press enter or click to view image in full size What did GitHub’s August 2026 outage show about retry behaviour? On 17 August 2026, GitHub was disrupted for 7 hours and 47 minutes, and the list of affected surfaces reads like the whole product: github.com, authentication, GitHub Actions, APIs, pull requests, issues and Copilot. Long day. Three days later, Vlad Fedorov, GitHub’s Chief Technology Officer, published The August 17 outage, and the work ahead . Read it. GitHub deserves real credit for laying out the mechanism that quickly, and the post also covers an earlier Actions incident on 6 August. The trigger was capacity. Traffic reached a new peak and a critical infrastructure component in the Central US data center failed to scale, which Fedorov states plainly: “Neither outage was caused by a code or configuration change. Both incidents were capacity failures at their core.” Recovery was different. Most services came back earlier that day, but some Copilot services took longer, and the post explains part of why: “Errors in those services triggered a client-side retry loop that increased traffic during recovery.” Read that sentence carefully. The retry loop did not cause the outage; it made recovery harder for some Copilot services.
